Even in its current barebones state, Thrive is already a great game with tons of replay value and potential for emergent gameplay. The game's main selling point is the Auto-Evo system, letting NPC organisms evolve and adapt to the environment much like the player would, which really makes the game world feel alive.
To borrow some examples from the game, in one playthrough you may take the role of a predator, and suddenly find that the cells you rely on for sustenance have evolved spikes to keep you from consuming them, forcing you to adapt to the situation by evolving some brand new weapons of your own.
Meanwhile, in a different playthrough, [i]you[/i] might take the role of a passive scavenger, evolving similar defense mechanisms to keep [i]yourself[/i] from being eaten. Likewise, changing atmospheric conditions may make your current design unsustainable and force you to adapt, either by finding a new source of energy or by moving to a different patch with different conditions. No playthrough of Thrive feels the same, due to every single choice you make having effects on the game world, whether they be small or large.
Still though, the game is not without its faults. While most of them are minor issues that don't really impact the game all too much and will for sure be fixed rather soon, there is one big issue that I feel takes you out of the process in a rather noticeable way.
The Auto-Evo system seems to really love cells which require multiple energy sources to survive, while heavily penalizing specialized organisms that can reliably thrive on just one of them. This goes against the common sense of picking a niche and sticking to it, which even the game tells you to do. This is largely an issue with the player organism, since the game uses the same Auto-Evo system to determine your own success. This causes some serious dissonance, because you may be doing well in the game as a specialized organism and the game will seemingly punish you for it, while paradoxically rewarding less effective gameplay styles. It should really be the other way around.
Still, even this is not enough to prevent me from giving this game an enthusiastic recommendation, since I am sure that this is a bug that will be ironed out way before the game's non-early-access release and not an intentional part of the game's design.
If this sort of game seems interesting to you, then you should definitely check it out!

Overall Thrive has a brilliant concept, and a fairly solid execution. However, it has two major flaws. Clarity, and optimization. Going in, even with the tutorials, its hard to understand exactly how the cells in the game function--as while there is explination on how build them, there is little to no explination for what you should be focusing on to keep your cells alive. Managing ATP is a grueling experience, but the end of my first run my cells had grown exponentially compared to others with dozens of glucose producing pieces to counteract the cost to keep the cell function. And even then, once your in the game, the cells seems to hemorrage glucose and atp despite the editor saying all clear.

Beyond that, the game starts to hemorrage frames once you start passing the tenth generation of cells. I'd found a niche for my first cells in a patch that was rich with iron, by investing heavily in rustolosis parts. i was, however, forced to move out of this patch not long after as my population rapidly began to climb in the 15-20k mark (in that patch alone) and obliterated my frames, making progressing a nightmare. I had to jump Patches every few generations, completely ruining the setup I had for my cells.

The game certain has a ton of potential, but it needs a /lot/ of work. A significantly more indepth tutorial, perhaps a dedicated tutorial mode rather than simple text boxes. The cell editing is fun, and the game is visually interesting and colorful. The concept of a spore evolution simulator that focuses on the details down to the chemical structure, rather than more fantastical elements, is fantastic and a great step for the genre--but it walks a razor thin line on being fun, and being too complicated.

Let me start by saying that I genuinely liked this game.  It has a lot of nice touches and the basic gameplay is a fun, if repetitive, experience.  That being said, I'm cognizant of the fact that my enjoyment of the game is likely due in part (perhaps largely in part) to the fact that it appeals to certain things about me that other players wouldn't share.  With that in mind, let me start with some more general comments.

Thrive is a "evolution" game in which you play a newly spawned cell that must evolve to survive and thrive (hence the title) in a variety of different environments while outcompeting others species of cells that spontaneously show up.  Do you remember Spore?  It's basically the cellular stage of that game, but with significantly more depth, better art design, and overall just not as shitty.  That being said, the basic gameplay of Thrive is pretty simple.  You control your cell, moving it around a largely featureless environment, occasionally running toward resource patches or running away from things trying to eat you.  The basic challenge of the game is ensuring you have enough glucose to generate ATP, without which you die.  Once a certain amount of time has passed (a process which can be sped up if you collect enough certain nutrients) your cell divides and you can choose to add a new feature like thylakoids which allow for photosynthesis, flagella which let you move faster, organelles which allow you to exploit new resources for energy, and so on.  Your goal is simply to continue surviving and grow your population faster than all your competitors, with the various upgrades allowing you to outcompete them.  It's not a particularly hard game, but it's relaxing and low-key and the sort of thing I like to play at the end of a long day to wind down.  So if you're into that sort of experience, then you might enjoy this on a purely gameplay level.

The other stuff I alluded to above is the depiction of biology, which is without hyperbole one of the most scientifically accurate depictions I've ever seen in a game (I'm a working biologist).  Well, almost.  I put evolution in quotation marks above because like most evolution games it bears essentially no resemblance to actual evolution.  Not that that's a criticism since actual evolution would be pretty boring to watch.  But the depictions of cellular biology and and basic ecology are actually really good.  All the cellular features are present in real cells and the game properly use ATP as the basic cellular energy currency, used not only for fueling your growth and basic cellular metabolism but also for powering your movement and some of the organelles that let you convert nitrogen to ammonia (needed for cell division) or spew gobs of slime at your pursuers.  So upgrading actually takes a bit of thought as you have to balance how new organelles will upset the energy and material balances of your cellular metabolism.  Because of that it's really not possible to load up on every type of organelle, so you inevitably have to decide what niche you intend your cell to operate in.  Will you be a photosynthetic organism, confined to the sunlit regions?  Will you exploit nutrient patches like iron and sulfur for energy and thus be constantly on the move?  Will you be a predator?  Again, the ecology is pretty basic, but what is there is present well enough that I really can't fault the game.

I conclude by saying that while I like Thrive, I'm also recognize that in some ways it's a game tailor-made for someone like me.  If you're not like me, it might not push all your buttons.  But if you are then you owe it to yourself to give it a try.

Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Thrive is a game that appeals to a logical, but over-stressed mind. The relaxation it provides is unseen with many other games that expect a player to jump in and immerse themselves in their proprietary universe. Thrive understands what it is. It saw the attraction that games like Spore and Plague Inc. and others alike and only aimed to enhance an aspect that it's predecessors lacked. 

It 'thrives' on it's simplicity; while yet, also its complexity. Though presented with problems (Like a lack of ATP production or overusing valuable materials.) the player is empowered to find solutions in whatever form they may come. You could develop alternative forms of energy that utilize various materials in your environment; or even abandon 'hunting and gathering' and utilize photosynthesis. Then again, that might be to the benefit of another organism who just might rely on the cell matter of those around them. Natural Selection, and Thrive is a game that has found a way to explore that idea in a brilliant fashion. To be the 'fittest' and to 'survive' and eventually 'thrive' had me fully enveloped in Thrive; and it shows well that, even once you think you've made it, there only seems to be more you want to accomplish.

There is no doubt though, that Thrive is in need of much more development; and being 'Early Access', that makes sense. Though entertaining, there are many occasions where it is obvious that content is lacking. Particularly when it comes to moving environments and late game experience. Though the goal is to purely evolve and slowly become more complex; it seems that there is a point where there's no further to go. In the worst of my play throughs, it felt like I was playing the old 'Agar.io'. Needless to say, it can get boring when it becomes an 'idle' game. 

That being said, the bare-bones are well established; and with a little more work, this is a game that could easily have a following akin to that of Spore. Given the issues above, it should be noted that none of them are due to design or developer error; they are merely symptoms of an Early Access game and that is nothing to put anything down. If anything, it is a sign that there is a golden road ahead and plenty of space for Thrive to take over a niche that is so empty in the gaming world. I for one am excited and I think the best sentence that I'd use to describe the game is -- Thrive is a game that is already an entertaining and enjoyable experience which empowers players to create, truthfully, whatever organism they'd like to; the development team seems to listen to the community and continues to improve what needs to be better while also never encroaching on the things that have allowed Thrive to, again, 'thrive' (I know I used the pun twice, it's funny shush)

SO. Thrive originally started like ten years ago from a bunch of people on the Spore forums, and it was all volunteers. As one might expect with free volunteers working on such an ambitious project, most ended up leaving. The game languished in development hell for years.

Recently, however, the remaining team opened themselves up for donations, and with that they were able to actually pay people to work on the game. The game itself is also still open source and anyone who can help is encouraged to do so. Today we're seeing progress updates every week on Thrive's website when before it'd be radio silence for months at a time, and it seems like they're keeping a consistent schedule. It's shocking how much development's sped up. Yeah, the game is just a microbe stage currently, but it's an actual game now, and damn if that isn't further than many people thought it'd go. It's short, but it's still fun to mess around with, and honestly I'd still be happy if they just perfected their cell stage and never moved on. My favorite Spore stages were always the cell and creature stages anyway, lol. 

The game is still actually open source and free, just like the original devs from the forums intended-you can download it from the Thrive website or their GitHub page. Buying it on Steam is just a way to support the continued development of Thrive. If you're curious about the game but not sure if you want to pay anything, you can download it from the devs, test it out, and then go ahead and pay for it here if you're interested in seeing the project go further. 

I'll continue watching Thrive's career with great interest.

Thrive is very hardcore in terms of biology, and really outdone spore in many ways.
However, I'd like to point out a few things to the Devs that makes this game less enjoyable than it should.

Your energy and resource systems have the right idea, but is really terrible balance wise. 

Waaay too much phosphorus is needed to reproduce. The direct result is that playing as algae sucks, since you still need to move around to collect this one resource that can not be produced passively. You should only need a tiny bit, and also be able to adsorb it from water. 

Glucose is so under powered. The bulk of the replication cost should be glucose (carbon source), but instead you don't need it at all to replicate. This is just weird and it encourages just slapping a pair of chloroplasts to meet the demand and be done with it. I expect food should be the number one resource everyone is pursuing and always not getting enough off, but instead food is so worthless in the current game.

Metabolic cost is stupidly high. Cells should be able to use little to no resource while staying still and doing nothing. The high metabolic cost is another reason algae is terrible to play. 

The editing screen is problematic in terms of evo points. You should be able to reproduce without going into the editing screen and accumulate evo points, and only go to the editor when hoping to do so. The current flat 100 points each is very frustrating to play with, especially when functional modifications of cells need more than that. This is especially true when trying to turn eukaryotic. The nucleus alone cost 100 points so you need to make a cell with extra of everything first and play with that terrible cell before adding a nucleus. 

Speaking of the nucleus, the current way of getting it is kind of dumb and misleading. You should be able to get mitochondria by engulfing other cells, and after that you should just be given a nucleus (and make it so that adding a nucleus does not instantly kill your metabolism)

About movement. It is very weird that bigger cells are so much slower. They should be less responsive but definitely not slower than smaller cells. It can be balanced by making big cells needing a lot more glucose to reproduce, instead of making them super slow.

In the end, I think it might be a good idea to implement a growth system. A new bar called protein or biomass, needs to be converted from glucose or maybe also with ammonia, affects size of cell, needs to be filled to divide, drops when taking damage, should generally be much harder to fill than the current ammonia and phosphorous bars. Although, it is understandable to have priorities and introduce growth in the multicellular stage.

Thrive is a spiritual successor to the cult god game/evolution simulator of 2008, Spore. Spore was rushed out of development and was pretty bare feature-wise, but nonetheless has a devoted, nostalgic following to this day due to its surprising replayability and niche. Both Spore and Thrive are divided into 'stages' of evolution, from simple cell to space-faring civilisation, but Thrive is looking to develop a much more complex and scientific representation of this. 

In Spore, you start in the cell stage as a cell which grows larger and evolves useful parts by eating food - eating food gives you 'DNA', and evolving new parts spends it. You can choose to be herbivorous, carnivorous, or omnivorous, and eventually you develop a primitive nervous system and clamber onto land for the creature stage. From there, you move on to a tribal stage, civilisation stage, and space stage.

In Thrive, on the other hand, you start as a cytoplasm in the microbe stage. You generate ATP via glucose and can evolve by absorbing ammonia and phosphate. Evolving new parts is a trade-off as you balance your ATP generation and expenses, as well as the overall population of your species; you are forced to find niches and adapt to your environment, both as an individual and as a species (unwise evolutions can starve your cell of ATP and lead to the extinction of your species). The next stage planned is the multicellular, which is intended to initially play similarly to the microbe stage but with even more complexity as you 'specialize cells of the colony, and later on divide the organisms into categories' before becoming 3D, and developing fully-fledged organs and a nervous system and progressing onto the 'aware' stage, then the awakening stage, society stage, industrial stage, and space stage. 

For such a small team, this is pretty ambitious. The microbe stage is intended to become even more complex (and currently suffers from performance issues), and from the descriptions given it seems that future stages will be even more detailed than this one. The industrial stage is, on the wiki, called a 'grand strategy'. This is all probably a very long way away. 

At such a cheap price, consider buying this game to be a donation to a dedicated dev team with a grand vision. I can't guarantee they'll succeed in making Thrive the game they want it to be, but I definitely want to be there for the ride, and am excited for all future updates.

This game is one more impressive than most. They try their best to make it super realistic, and I believe they've succeeded in that. At the time of this review there are 2 functional stages, Unicellular and early Multicellular. There is a Multicellular stage technically but you cannot save in it currently and it is very primitive, so make it 3 stages total. 

In the unicellular stage you are a single celled organism that must thrive in a possibly challenging world, with many different "clouds" of gas around you. You must live off these clouds and look for 2 specific ones as well, Ammonia and Phosphate, as if you get enough of it you are allowed to evolve. There are many different things you can attach to your cell to make it how you want. There is different patches for you to start out in and move to after you start. The best part about those is that you have to evolve to those patches as well as you're usually not suited to live in them. Eventually you get to the nucleus, which allows a bunch of new parts including things like the Binding Agent, which means you can create a colony by binding cells together. This leads to the next stage.

The early multicellular stage is pretty straight forward, sadly. Not much new stuff here. You are a normal cell, except an interesting twist: Your parts are other cells. You have to make and customize new cells to be apart of your colony and once you're out of the editor, you have to collect resources to become the colony. You spawn with a colony, but don't mistake it as a bug that you're not apart of it, because you have to grow. You are a bud that has to collect resources to grow other members of the colony onto you. Eventually, you get enough to become a true multicellular organism.

As of now, this review stops. The multicellular editor (Don't mistake it for the EARLY multicellular editor!) is a primitive 3D editor. As of now it is non-functional and you cannot save. It's interesting to experiment with the 3D aspect though. Your cells aren't models of the cells you made, but just spheres that are based off their color. Obviously, this is because it's unfinished, but there may be a small chance that those little balls that take the place of the cells stay.

Thrive is an amazing game, you should get it, even if it's unfinished.

TL,DR: Thrive is slowly but surely becoming a realistic version of Spore. It will (probably) get frequent updates and bug-fixes. It's probably going to be a lot more fun for people who want something more complex than Spore and/or understand a bit of biology. Or maybe they're just smart about life or something?

Welp, It's been a 16th years since Spore was released and there was no games like it, no good opponents... Untill now... When I saw this game for my 1st time i thought "What? What is this game? Is this a forgotten indie-game with lack of funds?". After this thoughts passed my mind I began searching an information, more information. I've found this game's steam page and wasn't surprised it still in deep early access even through 3 years of development. Also i was surprised on how cheap this game was. After i realised what this low price were set to be honest with gamers(because "Our game is in EA and we are only getting close to finish 1st stage of it, so we don't want to make the price big, instead we will increase it with future updates") I've decided to buy it. Okay, that was a long pre-history. What can we say about the game itself?

- Graphics — they are normal. Not the best we could get, but pretty beutiful and fullfiling it's purpose. I would give it 10 out of 10 for now. 

- Gameplay — pretty good. Currently you can play only 2 stages without critical bugs and only 1 of them filled with content. These two stages is a microbe stage(filled with content, closest to finish right now) and multicellular stage(pretty far from finish, already playable, but clunky and a bit boring). And, while playing on microbe stage, I should say IT'S WONDERFUL. It's kinda hard at start and require some basic understanding of biology(BUT don't worry, you'll get very useful guides and, if you'll follow them — you'll reach success), but after you get used to core mechanics, the game begins to feel pretty fun. You begin as simplest lifeform: a microbe without cellular core. Just a bunch of specialised organellas. Your gameplay is highly instinctive: absorb chemicals, don't get dead and absorb smaller microbes. Later you evlove, you gain your cellular core and a bunch of more difficult organellas. From that point you must understand and decide what your organism will be: predator or prey. Plant or animal. You can easily choose one or two specialities, but the game itself and I would highly recommend to not do it. It will make you multi-task, but you won't be good at any specialised tasks at all. I felt it on multicellular stage, where I couldn't normally evolve, because I prefered to hunt and gather iron to produce energy and I haven't added any of enzyme-creating organellas, so I wasn't able to hunt most of microbes in my biome and had to survive on my own. After this short story you could get a bit of understanding how the session goes in this game. The gameplay is perfect in my opinion, but i would highly recommend devs to increase the intellegence of NPC-microbes, because you can evolve too fast and become an alpha-predator, which leads to extinction of any creatures in your biome and, extinction of yourself in long future. I've met the situation where my microbe ate all of it's opponents and we have to move on the other biome. I give 8/10 to gameplay of microbe(since it's the only almost-finished stage)

- Sound and music. It's good, music is relaxing, but sound itself is a bit uncertain: sometimes you hear processes out of your FOV and that just annoying. 

- Atmosphere and some kind of plot — not added yet. But it looks like we could reach the space age at the end of the game. 

I HIGHLY RECOMMEND this game to everyone who enjoyed the Spore and give this game 8/10 for now: it needs some improvements, but already enjoyable.

So I've been following this project for a good 4ish years now, and let me say, development has ramped up extremely the last 2ish. I don't remember whom I got recommended this game by, but I sincerely want to thank them. 
PROs: The AI is amazing. Honestly the best I've seen for a game like this. The other creatures will genuinely try to find a way to "counter" your species. When I tried to become a huge basically primitive plant sea cow, everything else was either too big to engulf, or two fast to catch. Not only that, but while playing, the other creatures would develop spikes along the most exposed parts of their body, NOT to attack, but simply trying to stop me from engulfing them.
The cell stage is really fleshed out now, it used to be extremely bare bones, I remember not too long ago it was practically just a prototype with not even a nucleus. Now you have actual goals to get to and the progress seems actually worthwhile. Get enough ATP production to actually afford a nucleus -> Get binding agents -> make a colony -> become multicellular. 
This feels like what spore's cell stage should've been like.
Now for the CONs: Yes, this game will never be finished. We will probably see the macroscopic stage soonish (I am not a dev, just that's what it seems like), but aware and the society stages after are most likely at least many years in the future. I hope development speeds up with more people supporting them and them being able to afford full time devs, but who knows.
The multicellular stage is a solid 5/10, I don't wanna trash talk it, it's good, but it just doesn't seem the best imo. It is fun designing the different parts of your cell, but in order to progress, you need to become big and beefy or strip your original cell's parts and risk dying the next time you leave the editor. I am not really sure how you would avoid being a big sea cow like my cells were, but I am sure there is a way. Other than that, you really don't unlock anything special by being multicellular, sure you have safety in numbers, but it still feels bare. The devs seem to be working on this stage the most right now, so there will probably be a lot more updates to this stage.
It takes a LONG time to go through both the multicellular and up to the macroscopic stage. The mutation points being capped at a hundred is a big hinderence in the multicellular, and if you want to specialize different cells and try and see the macroscopic stage, it is going to take a few hours. This does make progression seem worthwhile, but it is still too slow imo. If there was a sliding mutation point cap in the options, that would be amazing.

Other than that, check it out for a few hours. It is a great evo game and is certainly worth the five dollars. Otherwise, keep an eye on the game

For those not in the know: 

Have you ever played EA's "Spore" and felt that for its grandiose scope, thought it felt shallow and lacking for what it seemed to be? 

That's because it is. 

EA's "Spore" originally belonged to Maxis games before they were bought out (the original creators of The Sims, Sim City, Sim Earth, and much more.) Spore was to be their magnum Opus. There goal was to start from an empty world as first emerging life, and fluidly continue that development all the way through a sprawling space age civilization. 

That vision was shared with many fans of Maxis's franchise, but when EA bought them out, they decided too much money had been "wasted" on this "silly" idea. They slapped googley eyes on Spore's creatures, shipped it as-is, and that was that. It was *okay*, it was still a more sprawling history than any game before, but it really lacked the depth, that was promsed by Maxis's vision. 

Thrive's goal is to realize this vision.

At the time I'm writing this, Thrive has just released their multicellular update, their first advancement to a 'next stage', showing they really are making progress towards that goal. Buy the steam version, support them on patreon, and the resulting game that will eventually come about will be like nothing you've seen before (well, okay, moderately like Spore, but way better.)

There’s a genre called popular science (sci-pop). It used to be in magazines, newspapers, and books, then later on YouTube in video format. And now, we’re starting to see games in this genre—which is awesome. I really like the concept and execution of Thrive. There are plenty of rough edges, but I understand that the game is still in early access, so I have no complaints about that.

However, there’s one issue that completely ruins the experience. And no, it’s not the unusual controls—those can be learned over time. The problem is the NPC AI.

You’d think that for tiny cells, an entire volcanic crater lake would be an enormous, nearly limitless world. And yet, despite there being only 160 individuals in the population, they all seem to be clustered around the player. My cell kept dying simply because my own species wouldn't let me move. They’d block my way, prevent me from reaching food, and constantly swarm around me.

I experimented with behavior settings—tried making them more sedentary, more active, even attempted to escape from them. And while I did manage to create some distance, the moment I stopped moving, dozens of my own species would suddenly appear from all sides. And I couldn’t even absorb them… but they could block me.

There are only 160 of us… so why does it feel so claustrophobic?

This issue frustrated me more than anything—being unable to reach resources because of my own kind. Because of this, I can’t recommend the game for now, but I really hope I’ll have a reason to change my opinion in the future.

UPD: I'm changing my rating from negative to positive because the developer responded to the issue, acknowledged it, and shared their thoughts on how the issue will be addressed. The game is still in early access, and with this kind of approach from the developer, I have no reason to keep a negative rating.

At its core, this is a simulation of single-celled life, and seeks to be a faithful representation of how life evolved on Earth- or how life [i]could have[/i] evolved on a pre-Cambian Earth.

If you're snooping this game, you more than likely know of Spore's cell stage, and perhaps wished for a game that injects more science and realism into it without compromising the fun of a video game. This is that game.

You directly represent a little blob of cytoplasm that's in a race against the clock to evolve before your yummy glucose is all gone. If time limits in this game stress you out, you may want to steer clear, as you will have, at most, about 1 billion years before your glucose-munching gel is virtually gone.

You must find a way to survive as your environment becomes populated with competing cells and, worst of all, toxic Oxygen; toxygen if you will.

Knowledge of biology is not required to enjoy this game, but will provide you some context and understanding of what is happening. Nerds can even calculate the math representing processes like glycolysis! With real mols!!

Currently the game encompasses single-celled life and a minor exploration of multicellular life, with the stated goal of eventually having a game where you can go from cell to ethereal being that shapes and manifests space-time.

Tempering expectations would be wise, but assuming the game only provides gameplay up to multicellular life, it still provides plenty of game to play. Anybody with an itch for science games, or "educational software" as some older folks know it, will have a ball controlling your little ball.

The game is available online for free, but the steam and patreon versions exist to help support the project even if you don't have the capacity to help on your own be it through art or through code.

Some of the reviews mention the game has been under development for a while or that the content for even the single celled stage is incomplete, and while some of that is still true, the rate of development recently went up drastically as the team could afford to hire a part time developer from all the support. As a result, not only is the single celled stage almost entirely finished, but the early multicellular stage (2-20 cells) has also begun development and is at the point of being in a playable beta, whilst the late multicellular where you start being a more conventional animal or plant has had work start on it's editor. All in all, I wouldn't be surprised if we saw early multicellular gameplay rolled out to the main version and out of beta sometime by the end of this year.

This game is early days, but at the moment the cell stage has the skeleton of what it needs to be a really fun spiritual successor to spore. I have easily spent 4 hours on this 4 pound game, though I would expect the price to go up if they add a macroscopic stage.
I love the more realistic, biology approach to making a cell. There is a lot more to to the editor then you first realise, as you can control sliders to change the membranes flexibility and change the cells behaviour. The familiar organelles are present, starting with the precursors which can later be swapped for mitochondira, chloroplasts, chemoplasts and vacuoles once you have a nucleas. Progressing is quite simple, you just have to find phosphate and ammonia until the lower left hand button can be clicked, then your cells can mutate.
The downsides to current gameplay is that you can only change small parts of your cell each time you divide (presumably to mimic the slow pace of cell evolution). You have 100 points to spend, but parts cost around 50 points each. The more stuff you add, the slower and more cumbersome your cell becomes and the more energy it needs to live, so it is a bit of a grind getting a cell to make its own glucose, turn it into ATP and still be fast enough to hunt other cells down. Chemoplasts can use hydrogen sulfide instead, but this is harder to find even in caves or vents than having chloroplasts make glucose in the top patches. Early game iron feels like the only viable energy source.
When you finally get to the multicellular stage suddenly you have twice as much to manage, mutating both individual cells and adding cells to your overall structure. Both take mutation points from the same pool, so making a complex 20 cell structure is really grindy. When macroscopic is added to the beta, people will probably make an ultimate stem cell and spam it. Turning as a multicell structure is faster than moving, and the only way to catch smaller cells. As you add cells you get much slower.

I am really hoping macrosopic stage brings you into a new map, as multicell is more taxing on the engine and micro. I really want this game to keep progressing, as what they have is good. If they can get to creature stage it could become a £20 game easily.

One of Thrive’s greatest strengths is that it’s fully based on real biology. Mixing and matching the different proteins, organelles, and other cell parts in the editor is my favourite part of the game. The amount of customisation and room to play around with the different cell components is very fun. The amount of management needed to make sure your cells actually Thrive instead of suffer is quite impressive, and I really enjoy the different patches you can go to. The amount of patches you can go to without causing harm to your species overall is at the moment quite limited, but I assume it will be elaborated on once the game comes closer to its 1.0 release. It’s a great simulator game that takes the concept of Spore’s cell stage and elaborates on it so well.

I never saw it manifest in any way. Until I randomly stumbled across a game called "Thrive" on Steam. The cell stage from Spore? I'm interested. Wait, the game is open source? That's a fascinating concept. Oh, it's five bucks? That's not bad at all. Let's check the Early Access section and see what they've said. Wait, 150 months estimated for early access? 

I was sold. Why? Because the devs of Thrive are clearly honest, open, and passionate about their project. Heck, when you start up the launcher for the first time, you get a little window telling you that they get that not everyone likes launchers, and that gives you options for either auto-closing the launcher or just starting without it entirely. Because these devs, quite clearly, [i]care[/i].

That care absolutely makes it into the game, as well. Some might call it feature light at the moment, but I ask to look with a discerning eye at the keen detail that's already there. Other games might, say, call things an environment shift and keep the same background. Other games might have "resource clouds" that once you gobble up a part of it, that's how it is. Not Thrive. Every new "patch" that you move your cell too gives off a different vibe and lighting. The "clouds" of resources? They spread out and dissipate, balancing out after a chunk having been consumed out of them. If this game was just a cheap, cobbled together attempt at crudely making something, those are details that didn't have to be added in. But they did. Because they care. 

All of this isn't even getting to the overall feel of things, the joyful experience of seeing that there's so much data provided to you to feel like you're really, actually witnessing the evolution of a planet. You don't [i]have[/i] to pay attention to all of the data it throws at you. You can gleefully keep what information you actually take in to a minimum if you want, or you can soak in what you find yourself interested in. It's not so much a game that says [b]you must[/b] actually fully comprehend cellular biology to go into it. It's more a game that simply uses elements of real life life to create a fascinatingly compelling journey through the evolution of it. Seeing those compounds I know, putting together a cell with slowly increasing complexity as I imagine it's potential future specializations and even evolution into a multi-cellular species? It's such a joy. 

Yes. That's what's in the game now. But that's not the entirety of this game's scope. Yes, the devs have placed pretty big promises about space faring empires, but I think it's more important to think about what that means, step-by-step. Don't focus on the empires. Focus on the fact of what it takes to get there. Even if this game only gets to the "creature stage" akin to what Spore had, it will still be utterly fascinating. And there's clearly the heart, care, and intent to take it as far as it can go, out past whatever horizons it can set its eyes on. I think that, for what the game is, presents itself as, and charges for on steam, that's more than respectable. It's a damn shame its not more well known, it's a damn shame that this game doesn't have some millionaire just say "hey, guys, here, have a wad of cash. Make the best game you can." Because from everything I can see, it deserves it, and so much more support.

[hr][/hr]

P.S. I've seen some posts complaining about difficulty. I'm not a min-max sort of person. I specifically even somewhat "roleplayed" my cell's evolution. Yes, there were times I lost an individual cell, and twice I was made extinct from a patch I just shifted to, but all the same I reached multi-cellular in a single day of playing. Take that as you will.

Great little early access game so far, really fun.  Devs putting tons of work into it.  Passively teaches you science even though you're just having fun designing your own evolution.  A few comments/suggestions for Devs: (Yes, I know you're already busy doing a ton!  But it's always good to have more feedback and suggestions)
- Endosymbiosis is to me the most fun part of the current game, but it's really broken.  The requirement to have to eat 3-4 other organisms and make it to the editor makes it virtually impossible - any species capable of eating another, wipes the other organism out entirely in that path within ~2 editor runs.  So halfway through progress the target species is extinct and you lose all progress.  After 10+ playthroughs and 30+ endosymbiosis attempts I've been successful twice.  Suggest either A) reduce number of editor runs required, B) increase AI cell count so more species exist at once and don't go extinct so quickly, (frankly, that is more interesting anyways), C) allow endosymbiosis progress to transfer to a different species (but same target organelle).  Or some combination thereof.
- Possible paths to evolution are currently: Iron, Glucose/Hydrogen sulfide consumer, or Photosynthesizer.  (Thermoplasts I can never get to generate enough - maybe that's just me).  And they are mutually exclusive in that Hydrogen Sulfide will not exist wherever there is light, glucose is not necessary to consume if there is light (except at night), thermoplasts won't work where there is light, etc.  And (correctly) per the tutorial, you should target 2 food sources to ensure you always have ATP.  So really there are only two viable paths to evolution - iron/hydrogen sulfide/thermoplasts, or iron/photosynthesis.  It's great that it's realistic, but it kills replayability quickly as it's just variations on a theme.  If we're getting out of Life As We Know It mode, there could be tons of options there to allow for wild sulfur-based life etc.
- Mutation Point system is...not great.  I understand there has to be some gating mechanism, but, something a bit more "organic" might be helpful.  Or letting some points transfer over (e.g. max of 15% carryover).  Or progression available towards unlocked items (e.g. show quest to unlock mitochondria).  I play on 0.9 multiplier because most organelles are *just* over what's required for 2 of them, which is fine, but I would prefer not to "cheat".

This is my second review on Thrive, as I decided tonight to do a fresh play through to play test the skeleton they have built so far. I think the cellular stage has definitely improved. Single celled is MUCH better, it feels way less revolved around a single thylakoid hex, and I didn't struggle at all to find enough compounds with the default settings. Once it gets to multi-cellular, however, we see a flaw. The different cell type system is a really interesting idea, but the transition is atrocious. It costs way too much mutation points to properly evolve multiple cell types, and even when you do, the massive speed decrease practically eliminates any predatory gameplay, and makes compound-seeking a nightmare. The strategy I found the most engaging was what I'd call the Scythe, in which you design your multi-cellular organism as a long stick protruding from the main cell, along with a hooked tip to the end. This design allows you to use rotational speed to efficiently engulf them, with the hook tip allowing you to "grapple" off iron chunks, providing even more speed. Cilia also seem to IMMEDIATELY lose any function after having two or more cells on your organism, which definitely keeps the Scythe strategy at bay, but, in a world without said strategy, would call for some annoying gameplay of hearing a loud stone grinding noise while rotating. Once we reach Macroscopic, I can't say theres really much room for review, it's very much a skeleton. I feel that the Awakening stages have IMMENSE potential, I love the direction the game is going towards that. I'm interested to see how they incorporate muscle cells, on if its going to be a "you need 5 muscle power to advance" or if we'll be tasked with developing our own muscular systems. I'm excited to see the proper implementation of Spore's Animal stage, as currently its a 3d space of nothing, and serves as a midpoint between 3d land and the Multi-Cellular. Thats my current thoughts on Thrive as of October 21st, 2023. To summarize, I'd like to see a cheaper, better optimized Multi-Cellular cell specialization system, faster turning/movement for Multi-Cellular organisms, maybe some AI-controlled Multi-Cellular organisms to hunt and interact with, and I'd like to see cannibalism, because god my own cells love to get in my WAY, please make them stop walking in front of me and taking my compounds, or let me KILL THEM, either one would be amazing. Like always, I appreciate the work you guys are doing, and I'm hoping this game becomes what Spore never was. Thank you for undertaking this, someday, I pray we see you at the finish line.

In light of the game's incredible strides in its development as of late, I've returned to update this review!

Out of all of the speculative evolution games that I've come across thus far, Thrive stands out as one of the most well-made and ambitious projects. The love for xenobiology and evolutionary biology bleeds through every single mechanic and devblog about this game and, although some sacrifices have to be made for the sake of an entertaining game, I believe wholeheartedly that this is one of the most realistic portrayals of microbiology on the market. 

Admittedly, Thrive isn't for the faint of heart, especially in the newer updates. It can be brutal and unforgiving for those that don't understand the basics of biology but even this will be mended in future updates with more rigorous tutorials. Even those that are familiar with Thrive can find it incredibly difficult to balance the ever-changing environments and its complex organisms but the addition of its more recent updates such as "miches" allow the ecosystem to be more rigorous and complex than ever, considering both the player's species and other AI species in terms of their ecological niche within the ecosystem. In the span of thirty hours, I don't feel like I've even touched the surface of what ecological niches are out there; due to the dynamic evolution and the multitude of organelles to combine to fulfill different playstyles, Thrive has near-infinite replayability that will only improve with time. 

I have no doubts that this is an incredible game that has been making greater strides than I'd ever expected, but I will admit that it is for a particular audience. Not everyone that liked Spore will like this game. However, anyone who loves xenobiology or speculative evolution, or just felt unsatisfied with the lack of realism in similar games such as Spore, will almost certainly love this game. It is the dream game for anyone that loves a scientific approach to evolution games and although it has slower development than an AAA studio, I can attest since buying it far back when multicellularity wasn't even on the horizon that it is well worth the wait.

This is a game that wants to be Spore. Development seems to have been going on for about a decade at this time of writing, but it only really started to pick up steam around 2019, according to the Github notes. So what do you get?

Do you remember the Cell Stage from Spore? That's pretty much what this game is. They say that they want to make all the Spore stages, but if you are a smart person, you probably know that you shouldn't expect anything substantially more than what's available right now for some time. So what does the Cell Stage have?

This game's Cell Stage (Microbe Stage according to the game) is pretty good. You begin as a tiny cell made of cytoplasm, and then you continue to expand into bigger and bigger cells. Like Spore, you swim around eating food, or other microbes. Engulfment is pretty fun - if your cell is bigger than the other cell, you can eat the cell by ramming it. Phototsynthesis is also pretty OP - it's free energy if you're in the right location, making the game pretty easy.

I wasn't able to figure out how the Auto-Evo predictor works. Apparently it has something to do with cell survivability? Not sure. I was bullying cells everywhere and my population still kept going down for some reason. I managed to beat the game despite this.

Speaking of beating the game, if you manage to survive for 20 generations, you win automatically. Cool. But in reality, beating the game right now means being able to assemble 5 of your cells together and choose to become Multicellular. This is how you reach the Early Multicellular Stage. Its editor looks pretty neat. Apparently you can make components devoted to some purpose and plug them together to create multicellular life. I didn't see the 4 extra free cells from the requirement to enter this stage, apparently they are part of your parent colony. When I tried to begin the stage with my new creature, it immediately fell apart, though apparently that's due to the "budding" mechanic. Still pretty neat though; colonies can be pretty OP.

The atmosphere is pretty nice. You can actually hear rain in the macroworld. And the backgrounds look amazing.

It's definitely a fine game to play for a few hours.

A wildly ambitious passion project that attempts to take the concept of Spore and implement it in much, much greater depth.  It is a work-in-progress and at the time of writing, only the microbial portion is playable.  Unfortunately, given the sheer scale of the project, I can't help but be skeptical that it will ever finish. 

Since getting it, there have been updates every few months that continue to move the project forward but by only tiny amounts.  I'm still giving this a marginal recommendation specifically to people interested in Spore-like ideas, but as a low-cost tour of an interesting idea that I do not expect to ever be fully realised.

This is what spore promised but failed to deliver.  The choices you make here have significance for your organism.  Its simple to learn and fun to play.  Its is short I have played thru in 3 times in 11 hours.  I think there are some more things to test out but this is not going to be a time swallower.  

Good things:  
- Easy to learn and experiment with.
- Well presented graphically
- Clear impacts from your choices and good info to help guide your choices.

Downside is that the evolve mechanic needs reworking.  
  1. to allow you to abandon a well developed organism and see how it prospers once launched. Moving to an interesting daughter while allowing the original to continue to prosper.
  2. to pivot more advanced organisms to enter new environments.
At present every change you make immediately affects all versions of you bacteria in every environment  even if two colonies are isolated.  And the inability to pivot more complex organisms to enter new environments greatly restricts the ability to move between biomes.  This is because you can't affect more than one or possibly 2 features a cycle and that is insufficent to traverse some biome boundaries.

There will also be a danger as this develops of keeping the simulation/ gameplay balance right, so far I think they have done a good job.  At £4 this is a worthwhile buy and its worth supporting the developers.

Thrive is a game about the wonders of life. The scenario is a simulated, Earth-like alien world, composed of different biomes, each containing different amounts of energy sources and resources. The story that is told, is the appearance, spreading and (through billions of years) diversification of life into different evolutionary lineages, courtesy of a pseudo-Darwinian evolution algorithm.

The role of the player in this story is to take control of a single evolutionary lineage, by strategically mutating their organism in an editor and determining towards which biomes it migrates. If the player's species is well-adapted enough to its environment and with respect to the other species, it will survive and its population will increase, achieving the "win" condition. If it is not, its species will be extinguished, resulting in the end of the game.

There are many different strategies to progress in the game, corresponding to different niches in a food chain. For instance, the player's species can either be photoautotrophs -obtaining energy from sunlight-, chemotrophs -obtaining energy from resources such as iron and hydrogen sulfide-, predators -hunting down other species to feed on them- or scavengers -feeding on dead organisms. Each of these 4 strategies offer a considerably different playthrough experience.

Do I recommend to buy this game? Personally, definitely, yes. Though, I understand that it may not be to everyone's taste.

If you enjoy relaxed, slow-paced games, which involve a certain level of strategic thinking, then Thrive fits perfectly for you. If you are a curious person, willing to have to think and learn some science while playing, and have the patience to explore all of its possibilities, it will give you many hours of enjoyment, even in the current version (v0.5.7, as I write these lines).

Moreover, by buying a copy of Thrive, you will be helping a development team that, with little resources and tons of passion and willpower, is continuously adding new features, slowly building the extremely ambitious final game.

Thrive in its current form only consists of the soon to be "finished" microbe stage, as well as the skeleton of what will be the future stages. It has some cool mechanics and its cell creation system is already much more in-depth than any other game I know, but it still needs to be balanced to make different choices more interesting and subject your cell to more varied environmental pressures with actual gameplay implications.

Thrive basically consists in moving around to eat blobs of differently coloured resources scattered around which are pretty much the same in terms of gameplay other than their usefulness depending on organelle choices.
As your cell grows, all resources with the exception of iron (which is very abundant around large chunks) become insufficient so your cell must find other ways to survive, such as engulfing other cells. While the basic mechanic consists on just running into other cells, the addition of sprinting made it more dynamic at the start of a run and pulling cilia later on. You can use "spikes" or toxins that you can "shoot" to kill your prey and then engulf its remains as well. However, doing this is much harder than simple engulfment and the reward not worth it. The system that handles AI evolution is very, very bad at the moment and cannot consistently make cells that are large enough to challenge you or make for good toxin/pilus targets.
A passive playstyle is also possible, but incredibly boring even as an incremental game as all you end up doing is sit next to an energy source and wait for the next editor cycle, then do the same thing all over again. You can spend hundreds of millions of in-game years licking the same iron chunk across multiple generations.

There are also other organelles that introduce new mechanics, such as binding to other cells to create colonies or giving simple orders to friendly cells. Their functionality is still rather unpolished and it appears the AI is incapable of using them for now.

Resources obtained allow you to grow and eventually evolve to customize your cell's design and increase the complexity of your species by adding organelles through the cell editor.
It is in this editor where my favourite part of the game lies. Here you build your cell organelle by organelle, spread to new biomes and adapt your species to them.
The cell stage is completely two dimensional, as if your cell(s) were being squished between microscope slides, although action is supposed to be taking place in large bodies of water. The amount of shapes cells and colonies can take on is rather limited in comparison to what exists in real life.
When it comes to the AI, it's not great, to put it simply. It constantly starves to death even right next to food sources and also has a tendency to fall really far behind as the game progresses regardless of difficulty settings, especially once you evolve a nucleus.

You have some agency over the behaviour of friendly cells through the use of sliders. I personally found this rather nonsensical and would prefer if it was just inherited from your own playstyle, with the enemy AI reacting to it with their own behaviour and mutations. Hunt a species a lot? it gains speed or defenses when it evolves.
In the current system there's little reason to make your species active, as friendly cells are often your biggest competition for resources and as long as you can stay alive population is a non-issue. The same thing goes for environmental tolerances, moving a slider bit by bit every generation is a chore that does not teach anything and should also be something that happens passively with each generation spent in the same biome.

The multicellular prototype is pretty bare-bones at the moment. However, being able to individually edit every single cell to create specialized clusters is already quite interesting if you have the patience to go through it. Unfortunately there's little gameplay reason to specialize cells when you can just stack a little of everything in a single cell type and spam it everywhere.

Each time you evolve, you have the option to expand your species to different environments. You can also save your cell (and any other cell on screen) by clicking on the "fossilize" button and try it in freebuild, Thrive's sandbox feature.

Visually it's nothing special, although some improvements are implemented from time to time. Cells feel excessively rigid due to the lack of procedural animations. Environments are mostly empty, look samey and do no significantly alter gameplay beyond resource availability. AI species look like a mess of randomly placed organelles and are not very visually distinct apart from their colour. There is an abundance of microstutters and occasional big stutters.

Is it worth the price in its current form? I don't know. However, it is open-source and you can download it for free on the developer's website so purchasing it is entirely optional. It's also only getting better and better with time. Thrive has been around in some shape or form for over a decade but it's only started to look like an actual game in recent years, with very slow progress yet impressive resilience.
I also believe it's a project that while already ambitious for an AAA studio, is gargantuan for a tiny team of developers dedicating their time to the creation of the game, so they will certainly appreciate your support. Perhaps, in the far, far future, Thrive will be able to become the Spore we never got, but the road ahead is still very long and very rocky.

I highly recommend this game for anyone disappointed by spore. It is very scientific. While the later stages are only prototypes (for now) the microbe, and early multicellular stages seem to be mostly complete. You can get it for free but I recommend actually paying for it here on steam because the devs are basically working for free. Also it is an open source project and you can join the dev team if you want to speed up progress.

TL:DR Scientific spore with 2 mostly completed stages and devs working for free.

For an alpha, of an alpha... it has better gameplay than some fully developed games that I've seen. The development team was not originally a studio, basically just a band of volunteers and college kids that wanted to play spore but actually realistic, and here we are so far. Still not out of the cellular stage, won't be for at least a few more years, won't be finished for maybe 10-30, but this game is just as realistic as real life. Unlike Spore, where you just get "parts", and add them to make your blob better, with cartoony eyes, which are actually multi-cellular constructs, you have a legit cell. Don't be fooled by the version, that's the version of the respective stage, so this isn't version 0.8.1 of the whole game, only the cell stage. Once we move beyond 1.0.0, that means multicellular development will begin.

Want to know why it is going to take so long, even now that the game has a full on studio and is getting good funding? The developers have to teach themselves biology, and parts of chemistry and physics. That's right, they'll all have science degrees before they get even near finishing the game, because the same people coding the game need to have intimate knowledge of how life works, from the bottom up.

You get a blob of plasma instead, completely empty. You can customize the cell membrane of it, each one has upsides and downsides, and there are some obvious choices like a cell wall if you're making a plant. From there, you need ATP. There's a bare minimum to survive, and a point where your cell is overstuffed and begins to divide itself, organelles first. When it completes that's how you enter the evolution menu, the cytoplasm fully divides in mitosis and you evolve the new generation.

EVERYTHING, uses ATP. Not at all like the zero upkeep "parts", these actual factual organelles all use energy, on top of needing it to move and even exist. Even the Mitochondria (baseline energy factory, takes sugar makes energy) has upkeep, it doesn't directly take ATP but each one has diminishing returns, and even reduces the total amount of energy you can make if you over do it. Evolving in this game isn't so much as based on what you want, as what you need, exactly how it is in nature. You have to endure the full process of homeostasis, if the water pressure is too high you squish, too low you separate apart, too hot you burn, too cold you freeze, radiation is bad (unless you can eat it) and a bad ph balance can dissolve you almost instantly.

Once you run out of glucose (sugar) in the environment, suddenly the game goes from all to easy, to fighting to survive. You have to either find a different way to harness the environment for survival, like converting iron particles through a rusting process (forgot the organelle name) for energy, taking in radiation like a little fission reactor, or there's even an organelle that makes ATP when you go from a hot part of the map to a much colder one, which I didn't even know was a real thing! Otherwise, you have to learn how to hunt, all of which can be done multiple different ways as well.

And don't forget about the AI. This is not like most games, where the AI is either a guide, a supplement for a real player, etc, this game's AI is trying to survive and thrive just as hard as you are. They start off evolving slow, only doing it in response to environmental changes, so they can either go long periods without evolving much, or periods where they completely change every generation. They split off from your initial plasma blob, since it's basically the first cell on the planet, meaning there's only a few AI in the beginning and they aren't that unique, but as the game goes on the planetary ecosystem gets exponentially more diverse and complex.

For every weapon there's a counter, and for every environment there's a way to make energy from it. Like I talked about earlier, or when I briefly mentioned making a plant, which is something you can do. Unless of course a competitor evolves an organelle to dissolve your walls, and then you. Makes sense that the easiest gameplay style has the hardest drawbacks and counters, so being a plant is more of an AI thing than a player thing, but it's an option. If you get poisoned, there's organelles that can make you partially immune, getting enough can make you fully immune, and eventually there will be multiple poison types each with their own cure.

The biggest goal of the game, as of 0.8.1 of the cell stage, is obviously going multicellular, but how? You need a Nucleus, which unlocks more complex organelles, but takes more ATP than probably the rest of your cell combined. After that, and getting to a stable enough point, you start dividing into a cell colony. This is where the game really starts to look nothing like Spore, and keep in mind this is all still in the first out of 5 or 6 stages planned for the game. Now, you don't just have to care for yourself, but [b] all, [/b] of yourself. If you don't have enough food to sustain the colony that's a huge issue, and you have to either shrink some or the game will shrink you for you. Once you get to a certain cell colony size, you can coalesce into the next plane of reality: Multicellular life. 

This, and every other stage, "technically" exist but are bare bones placeholders. Multicellular though is more fleshed out than the rest ofc, since it's the next one, but it's also vastly different from Spore. Who knows what it will look like in the future once it starts getting worked on, or when it's finished, but what I do know is where Spore gives you a little goober that you make bigger on land with different parts, in this game you are going to start just as realistic. 

I imagine probably becoming like a jellyfish or something, since that's the first multicellular creature along with early forms of "proto-plankton", because they have a similarly gelatanous body and food requirements, first getting it from their environment, and then possibly getting it from others. Evolving organs or your body shape, or who-knows-what-else is also going to likely be the same vibe as organelles, where everything takes energy, and has upsides and downsides you need to carefully balance. Even just thinking about real life, we really don't know what could happen, because every evolution at that point was a magical feat. Fins, skin, and then scales, I imagine where the cell stage was somewhat linear, this is the point where you really get to customize yourself. 

There's a different between "multicellular life", and "animal", so where Spore is basically stage 2, 2A, and 2B of life smushed into just stage 2, this game does the process justice. Similar to how you start as a cell in stage 1, stage 1A is getting the nucleus, and stage 1B is becoming a cell colony. Getting on land is going to be a feat similar in scale to getting a Nucleus, without any immediate benefits, requiring an already stable enough creature, but broadening your horizons to the next level.

Who knows? Maybe the game will be full on, truly almost sandbox style, like Spore but completely realistic. If that's the case, then you could stay in the water and evolve fish people, or become a bug, a parasite latching onto another creature and feeding off of it's success, a dinosaur, a bird, the possibilities are endless! These devs also want to ambitiously go way beyond, after going to space and becoming an empire there will be an "Ascension stage", that might just be winning, or a sort of new game plus.

Thrive is among the most terrible, slow, and absolutely boring games I have ever played…
I simply must review it, if only to warn others away.

Note: I play many games, and I show the ones I like.
I will not show Thrive.
Why?

Well, let’s keep this organized.
Please let me know if anyone thinks this is off-base or un-fair, as I will attempt to accurately and descriptively outline precisely why I find Thrive to be among the worst of the functional games I have ever play, and I have played a great many….

[b]Suggestions:[/b]
[h1]1: What A Terrible Start…[/h1]
You start as a slow, boring blob, and all you can seemingly do, is slowly dive through clouds…
Oh, you can sprint, but that burns your energy, which you need to get out of this super slow, terrible intro part of the game.
It is so profoundly boring…
It really begs the question: why would anyone include this in the game?
It is so obviously un-fun, yet it is here.
I strongly suspect ‘fun’ might not have been the primary objective here, which is an outright damning condemnation of any game, as it represents a fundamental failure of grasping what a game is supposed to be: a game is supposed to be fun!

[u]I know ‘fun’ can be subjective, but it seems many of the positive reviews here seem to focus on how fun the game will be, not how fun it currently is, which is a glaring red flag for me.[/u]

[h1]2: Why is the Zoom So Slow?[/h1]
Speed this up please!

[h1]3: Why is the UI So Big and Bloated?[/h1]
I do not need to constantly see a giant “Environment” bar, just sitting there, uselessly taking up a good chuck of my left screen.
The “Compounds” bar also needs to go.
In an attempt to turn this bloat off, I looked up “Graphics” and by “GUI” but all that is there is a line, that does nothing…
I must say: if immersion is what you were going for, these two big, blocky chunks tank it badly!
Let the player minimize, or outright turn the screen bloat off, perhaps via a little X in the corner or something, maybe having it turn into another little letter / icon on the lower left.
After all, you already have 9 of them, what’s 2 more compared to the current obnoxious UI monstrosity?

[h1]4: Default Control Scheme Feels Terrible![/h1]
[b]It has wasd movement, but if you dare to use the mouse, it instead makes whatever key you were pressing move towards the curser instead![/b]
It feels terrible to play!
I did not find the option for a more sensible and expected control scheme here.
Does it even exist?
 
[h1]5: All That Build-up, For This?[/h1]
So, after a profoundly slow and boring time of wandering around gas clouds: I get to do what the game should have opened with.
Too bad it’s also boring!
It all breaks down to picking what you want to try and eat, and how slow you are willing to tolerate going in exchange for hp.
I already mentioned above how slow you are already right?
[i]Now, imagine being even slower![/i]
Ya, that’s sounds absolutely terrible, right!
It is!

[h1]6: No Point Saving Up…[/h1]
You get 100 Mutation Points each generation, so no point saving up, as you never get more…
This means it is NEVER advantageous to put off mutation, removing a great deal of potential depth and player decision making.
[b]An odd decision, to disincentivize thinking ahead and planning, in a game that one might think would be all about that![/b]

[h1]7: Terrible Combat Too?![/h1]
At first, I was like: Where is it?!
Then, it appeared.
I was randomly engulfed!
You just randomly get engulfed by fly-by randos and can’t do anything about it…
Terrible!
All you can seemingly do is literally wait for the end, or flat out suicide. 
Yep, there is a literal suicide button on the UI!
Wow…

[h1]8: Is that a Turd?[/h1]
I think it is…
Oh, I’m sorry, I’m just slowly drifting through the microbial clouds trying to keep my boring, circle blob from dying or being randomly ambushed, and I saw it.
A big, brown lump, just floating there… 
A very fitting representation for Thrive, as a big lump of crap was exactly what I was thinking in terms of how to best describe this game.
It’s a big, boring, lump of crap.

[h1]So, to summarize:[/h1]
Thrive is slow, downright ponderous to play.
Its UI is a grotesque, obnoxious monstrosity.
It has terrible combat.
It has terrible exploration.
What then, does Thrive offer?
Pain.

Now, perhaps Thrive has some value as a study aid for microbiology students, or others somehow fascinated by the super slow, super small crap world, but assessed strictly as a game, it is in my opinion a terrible one.

It crashed and I though it busted my graphics card before I rebooted. I won't be playing it anymore (out of Cowardice) which sucks because I liked those thirty minutes. Either way, don't expect the microbe gameplay to be super engaging; in that aspect the game is essentially a spore cell stage with Darkest Dungeon RNG, which is to say you either rationalize it as an immersive feature that you are lost in a void between clouds of edible stuff or you think it's bullshit. I'm a big nerd, so I was in the former group before joining the third group of refunding a science simulation because I'm scared of it murdering my graphics card in cold blood.

[h2]Some Gameplay Comments:[/h2]
The gameplay's real focus is on the evolution of your species and carving out a niche successfully. This means that like in real life (unless I'm wrong, in which case be sure to insult me in the most immature way possible), the biggest pressure to grow massive is either to eat bigger things or give predators a hard time eating you, though every ecosystem has room for rodents and rabbits and this is probably why many people complain about feeling the game practically restricts them to small and efficient microbes. I wish I could give a more developed opinion on this, but my own experience was pretty well summarized by the two prior points. 

[h2]My Playthrough:[/h2]
When I first started the game, and I felt like growing big enough to get a nucleus, since that's when all the cool stuff starts happening. Glucose was the only available food source at the very beginning of the game, but as the game progressed it's common consumption by every species of microbe led to it being far rarer then it used to be. There were nice graphs to help me see this in the mutation/evolution UI. This made it so I decided to specialize into Iron, since it seemed like a consistently available and under-exploited food source. I also added a flagellum to swim faster, which came in use when I found that another cell had grown large enough to predate on my own. They offered me the superior mobility necessary so that my previously much slower species only lost 2/5 of it's population instead of 5/5 of it's population. I then prioritized size increase and a membrane upgrade to prevent it from easily engulfing or destroying my cell, and then my game crashed. Right as it was starting to get interesting for me too.

[h2]Performance Gripes:[/h2]
The Graphics are alright, good considering the nature of the project, but not something that I would describe as "Murdilate your graphics card" good, especially since I turned of something that was making my framerate take a serious drop on the title screen. I don't know if you can optimize that out or what, but I used a gaming laptop, not a macbook from 2010, so I feel the graphics were punching well above their weight class in the ring against my graphics card. this is all considering me disabling 3D backgrounds (At least I think I did. If I didn't then I'd really like to know where in the UI the option was)

[h2]Something Resembling a Conclusion:[/h2]
Altogether, I still support this project (though I am doubtful of it ever finishing) and wish I could have gotten farther before a combination of presumable spaghetti code and my own lack of spine (though perhaps it's reasonable to not risk paying 205 dollars just to play a game that's damn near a demo). I can't recommend this with the freeze into crash into fake out GC death, but if you are more confident in your PC then me then give it a try. I especially wish I could have gotten to the part where you can begin inter-cellular cooperation and start creating larger lifeforms, since that sounds like they are trying to smooth out the distinctions between the stages, as opposed to spore choppily going from cell to complex terrestrial life-form to caveman to tanks to space empires. I kinda hope they aren't doing that though, because that sounds legitimately impossible and like they'd be working for the next 50 years just to get to jellyfish.

This is a surprisingly thin evolution simulator. I believe this is probably due to it being developed as a hobby. The gameplay is just... tedious. Floating through massive empty areas to find oval shaped blobs of various nutrients is pretty boring. And evolving to add new modules / organelles is often counterproductive. You can quickly bog your organism down with weight and passive ATP drain that, even when you're attempting to specialize to a particular environment, you end up slow, recovering fewer resources, and performing worse than your 5 or 6 part sized organism that you evolved within the first ten minutes. 

So, I suppose that's my main complaint. You can quickly evolve into the most efficient organism for a particular environment before you start regressing as you get larger. So I felt a large pressure into staying as a very small organism, no matter the environment. There is some challenge when venturing to other biomes - you'll need to rapidly evolve to remove older components while adding environment specific one for this environment... but after that, you're stuck in a small organism. Evolving more to become larger and more complex yield dramatically reducing gains, until they start becoming a hindrance. I just don't feel like it promotes building a bigger and stronger and more specified, or general, organism.

And... there's just not much to it.

Oh, and did I mention the gameplay is boring and tedious? Literally half of my new games end with me running out of glucose and dying before I find even the first blob of glucose. And that takes several minutes. Usually the new game starts off with: wander an empty void for 3-4 minutes before you run into glucose for the first time. From a gameplay perspective, this is just horrendous. And the later game is no different. Minutes at a time of wandering vast voids before coming across resources. It's just not fun.

You get punished for making bigger and cooler cells because the amount of time to split and thus evolve is increased exponentially. It's much more efficient to make a tiny cell and just swim around with one passive producer. You can't rely on players not doing that because players WILL optimize all the fun out of a game, the only thing a dev can do is delay that as long as possible.

I figured out how to make my cell "survive and thrive" on every level. To gain access to photosynthesis proteins, you have to migrate to those patches with more light. It's a little hard but as long as you store enough resources (like iron) and make it to the first evolution, you'll gain access to photosynthesis proteins.

I expected a more realistic life simulator with complicated biochemical reactions. Pity that it still uses HP and DNA points, just like every other game. Even the engulfing process is just a button. And why can't I get any ATP by digesting other cells?
... but perhaps I'm requesting too much since the performance problem starts to appear even without what I have wished for.

Anyway, this game is essentially a level-up rogue-like survival game and it's still under development. It should not be called a simulator.
